title: Timber Valley Landscaping: equipment purchase on credit, income statement effect and accounting equation
participant_role: CPA advising the owner of Timber Valley Landscaping on an equipment purchase
judge_role: Owner of Timber Valley Landscaping deciding whether to buy a new piece of equipment on credit
scenario:
You are to assume the role of a CPA for Timber Valley Landscaping. The owner (judge) is trying to decide if she should purchase a new piece of equipment. She has asked you for advice so she can make a financially sound business decision.

The new piece of equipment will cost $50,000 and will last 5 years. The owner has indicated that the equipment will allow the business to generate $50,000 more in sales each year. The Owner (judge) wants to purchase the equipment on credit. Show how adding the new equipment will affect Timber Valley's Income Statement and Owner's Equity for the next two years. Break down the purchase of $50,000 of equipment on credit into debits and credits using a general journal that you create. Explain to the owner how the purchase of equipment will affect the accounting equation and ultimately the Balance Sheet.

You will present your recommendation to the owner (judge) in a role-play that will take place in the owner's office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendation and have answered the owner's (judge's) question, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: If the equipment were purchased for cash (instead of a loan), how would this affect the accounting equation?
How would a useful life of 10 years for the equipment affect the decision?
How does an increase in income affect Owner's Equity?

solution.overview: A strong answer shows that the equipment adds $50,000 of sales and $10,000 of straight-line depreciation each year, so net income and owner's equity rise by $40,000 in each of the next two years. It records the credit purchase as a debit to Equipment and a credit to Accounts Payable, shows that assets and liabilities both rise by $50,000 so A = L + OE stays balanced, and explains accounts payable, the accounting cycle and the advisory role of a CPA.

by_task.task: Income statement and owner's equity effect (two years)
answer: Annual depreciation = $50,000 cost / 5 years = $10,000 per year
Year 1: sales $50,000 minus depreciation $10,000 = net income $40,000
Year 2: same, sales $50,000 minus depreciation $10,000 = net income $40,000
Net income flows into owner's equity, so equity increases by $40,000 each year ($80,000 over two years)
Recommend the purchase because the added income far exceeds the yearly cost of the equipment

by_task.task: General journal entry for the credit purchase
answer: Create a journal with at least account titles and debit and credit columns (date, source document and posting reference columns are optional extras)
Debit Equipment $50,000
Credit Accounts Payable (or another liability) $50,000

by_task.task: Accounting equation and balance sheet effect
answer: Assets increase by $50,000 (Equipment) and liabilities increase by $50,000 (Accounts Payable)
Because both sides rise by the same amount, Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity stays in balance
Owner's equity is not changed by the purchase itself, only by the income the equipment later earns
Accounts payable is a liability, an "IOU" to the vendor
The business owes the money now and must repay it in the future

by_task.task: Role of a CPA and the accounting cycle
answer: A CPA advises the owner on how business decisions affect the company's financial position; the final decision stays with the owner
Accounting cycle: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare a worksheet, prepare financial statements, record adjusting and closing entries, prepare a post-closing trial balance
The cycle repeats monthly and yearly so management gets timely financial information, and every transaction ends up in the financial statements

calculations.label: Annual depreciation (straight-line)
steps: $50,000 cost / 5 year useful life = $10,000 per year

calculations.label: Income statement effect, Year 1 (and Year 2)
calculations.result: Net income increases $40,000 each year; owner's equity increases $40,000 each year

judge_question_answers.question: If the equipment were purchased for cash (instead of a loan), how would this affect the accounting equation?
answer: Equipment (an asset) increases by $50,000 and Cash (an asset) decreases by $50,000
Net effect on total assets is $0
No effect on liabilities or owner's equity

judge_question_answers.question: How would a useful life of 10 years for the equipment affect the decision?
answer: It would make the purchase more attractive
The $50,000 cost would be spread over 10 years instead of 5, so depreciation drops to $5,000 per year and net income rises to $45,000 per year

judge_question_answers.question: How does an increase in income affect Owner's Equity?
answer: Increases in income increase owner's equity
Net income is closed into the owner's capital account at the end of the period

key_concepts.definition: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. Every transaction keeps the two sides equal.

The repeating steps of accounting: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare a worksheet, prepare financial statements, record adjusting and closing entries, and prepare a post-closing trial balance.
The book of original entry where each transaction is recorded with the date, account titles, and debit and credit amounts (debits listed first).
A liability representing money the business owes to vendors for purchases made on credit, an "IOU" that must be paid in the future.
Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset evenly over its useful life. Annual depreciation = (cost minus salvage value) / useful life; here $50,000 / 5 = $10,000 per year.
Revenues minus expenses for a period. Net income increases owner's equity; a net loss decreases it.
The owner's claim on the assets of the business (assets minus liabilities). It rises with owner investments and net income and falls with withdrawals and net losses.
Buying an asset now and paying later. Assets and liabilities both increase by the same amount, so the accounting equation stays balanced.
A certified public accountant advises business owners on the financial effects of decisions, but the decision itself belongs to the owner or manager.

notes: The PDF solution shows only the Year 1 income statement effect (sales $50,000, depreciation $10,000, net income $40,000); the Year 2 figures in the solution repeat the same numbers because the scenario gives constant sales and straight-line depreciation. The judge answer about a 10-year life says only that it makes the purchase more attractive; the $5,000 and $45,000 figures are derived arithmetic.
